tasks.prompt: Order the steps for preparing distribution records ahead of the annual Ministry inspection.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The inspection covers sampling, adverse incidents, maintenance programs and operator certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: records for the full distribution system for the previous calendar year.

cards.label: Pull the sampling completion record and reconcile it against the regulatory schedule
Compile every adverse incident file with its notifications, resamples and closure records
Summarize the flushing, valve and hydrant program completion against their targets
Verify the certification and training records for every operator who worked on the system
Correct any record gaps found and note the corrections honestly in the file
Brief the inspection team members on where each record set is kept

tasks.explanation: Reconciliation comes before compilation: an inspection finds gaps either way, and finding them first allows honest correction. Certification is checked as a record set of its own, and the brief ensures the person asked can actually produce the record.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for responding to early signs of nitrification in a warm storage facility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The system uses chloramine at the treatment plant and summer temperatures are high.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one reservoir showing falling chlorine residual, rising nitrite and falling pH over three weeks.

cards.label: Confirm the pattern by resampling for residual, nitrite, nitrate, pH and ammonia at the facility
Increase the facility monitoring frequency and add an upstream and a downstream site
Boost turnover by lowering the operating band so stored water is replaced faster
Flush the low residual mains downstream of the facility
Coordinate with the treatment plant on the chloramine residual and ammonia balance leaving the plant
Track the indicators weekly and return to routine monitoring only after they stabilize in the normal range

tasks.explanation: Nitrification announces itself as a pattern across several indicators, so confirmation uses the full set. Turnover and flushing attack the stored, aging water where the bacteria grow, plant coordination addresses the chemistry feeding it, and weekly tracking decides when the episode is truly over.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for starting up a chlorine booster station in a distant zone.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. Residuals at the zone extremity have run below the target range each summer.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a new booster chlorination station at a reservoir serving the far end of the system.

cards.label: Confirm the chemical storage, feed equipment and safety systems pass their start up checks
Set the initial dose from the measured incoming residual and the zone target residual
Start the feed at the low end of the calculated range and confirm the pump delivers
Sample downstream at set travel times to confirm the residual rise arrives as expected
Adjust the dose in small steps until extremity residuals sit inside the target range
Record the dose settings and add the station to the chemical inventory and inspection rounds

tasks.explanation: A booster station is commissioned like any chemical system: safety and delivery first, dosing second. Starting low and sampling at travel times respects the delay between dose and effect, and the station enters the standing rounds so it is managed, not forgotten.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for adjusting a booster chlorination dose after extremity residuals decline.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. Incoming residual from the treatment plant has not changed over the same period.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one booster station whose downstream residuals have fallen over two weeks.

cards.label: Verify the current downstream results by resampling at the extremity sites
Check the booster chemical tank level, pump delivery and injection point condition
Check whether zone demand or tank turnover changed and increased water age
Raise the dose by a small step and record the time and the new setting
Resample downstream after the expected travel time and compare with the target
Continue small adjustments or escalate to a water age investigation if residuals do not respond

tasks.explanation: Resampling separates a real decline from a sampling error, and equipment checks separate a feed problem from an age problem. Dose changes are small and timed to travel time, and a dose that stops working is treated as a symptom worth investigating, not a number to keep raising.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for designing the annual flushing program at system scale.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. Complaint records, residual results and main age data are available for planning.
tasks.configuration: Scope: the whole distribution system, combining unidirectional flushing zones and dead end flushing.

cards.label: Rank areas by complaint history, residual performance, main age and known dead ends
Divide the ranked areas into flushing zones that work from the clean source outward
Assign each zone a method, unidirectional flushing for looped areas and blow off flushing for dead ends
Estimate water volumes, crew days and disposal needs for each zone
Publish the program calendar with customer notification lead times for each zone
Set the residual and clarity targets that will judge each zone complete

tasks.explanation: Ranking puts scarce crew time where the evidence says water quality needs it most. Zones still work from clean water outward, volumes and disposal are planned before hydrants open, and completion targets are set in advance so success is measured, not felt.

tasks.prompt: Order the leadership steps after a flow reversal discolours water across several neighbourhoods.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The reversal was caused by an emergency shutdown that changed flow directions for several hours.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a large area with brown water complaints following an emergency valve operation.

cards.label: Confirm the cause and that normal flow directions and pressures are restored
Map the complaint area and identify the mains that carried reversed flow
Flush the affected mains starting from the clean source toward the complaint area
Advise customers to run cold taps after their street is flushed and to avoid hot water use until then
Sample residuals and clarity at the worst affected streets during the flushing
Close the event only when complaints stop and samples confirm normal quality, then file the event review

tasks.explanation: Flushing before the flow pattern is normal again would waste the effort, so restoration is confirmed first. Flushing follows the same clean to dirty direction as the program work, customer advice is timed to their street, and closure waits for both complaints and samples to clear.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for building a dead end management program for the whole system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. Dead ends are scattered across old and new areas and have never been managed as one program.
tasks.configuration: Scope: an inventory and flushing program covering every dead end main in the system.

cards.label: Extract every dead end from the system maps and verify the list in the field
Rank the dead ends by residual history, complaint record and number of homes served
Fit or assign a flushing point, hydrant or blow off, to every ranked dead end
Set a flushing frequency for each dead end based on its ranking
Add the schedule to the work management system with completion tracking
Review residual results at the worst dead ends each season and adjust frequencies

tasks.explanation: A program starts with a verified inventory, because maps alone miss field reality. Ranking ties flushing effort to measured risk, frequencies become tracked work rather than memory, and seasonal review adjusts the program to what the residuals actually do.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for investigating a chlorine residual decline across one zone.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. Plant finished water residual and zone demand are both unchanged over the period.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one zone where extremity residuals fell steadily over a month.

cards.label: Plot the residual results by site and date to find where the decline starts
Check storage turnover and operating bands for the zone facilities
Check for recent valve changes that may have lengthened the flow path to the weak sites
Inspect the weak area for dead ends, low use mains and recent construction
Apply the corrective action the evidence supports, such as band changes or flushing
Resample the weak sites on a fixed schedule until residuals recover and hold

tasks.explanation: Plotting by site and date turns a zone problem into a location: the decline starts somewhere. Storage and valve changes are checked before pipes are blamed, the correction matches the cause, and recovery is proven on a schedule rather than assumed.

tasks.prompt: Order the leadership steps for investigating a cluster of taste and odour complaints.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. No treatment plant process change has been reported in the same period.
tasks.configuration: Scope: twenty similar complaints from one part of the system over three days.

cards.label: Log and map the complaints with the exact words customers use for the taste or odour
Collect samples for residual, turbidity and general chemistry from the complaint area
Check recent work in the area, including flushing, breaks, new mains and valve operations
Compare results with the treatment plant finished water record for the same days
Flush or adjust operations in the area if the evidence points to distribution causes
Reply to every complainant with the finding and keep sampling until complaints stop

tasks.explanation: The customers own words are diagnostic, so they are recorded exactly and mapped before samples are taken. Recent distribution work is as likely a cause as the plant, both records are compared, and every complainant receives the finding because silence reads as indifference.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for implementing a storage turnover improvement program across several facilities.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. Water quality results show the oldest water at the facilities with the smallest swings.
tasks.configuration: Scope: five facilities whose daily level swings are too small to refresh stored water.

cards.label: Measure the current daily level swing and estimate the water age at each facility
Set a target swing for each facility that balances water quality with fire storage and pump limits
Lower the top of the operating band or deepen the drawdown in small steps at one facility at a time
Monitor residuals at each facility outlet after each step before moving to the next facility
Lock the proven bands into the operating sheets and SCADA alarms
Report the residual improvement to management after one full season

tasks.explanation: Age is measured before bands are moved, and targets respect fire storage rather than chasing quality alone. Changing one facility at a time keeps cause and effect clear, proven settings are locked into the sheets and alarms, and a season of data makes the report.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for verifying and closing out a completed flushing program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. Zone crews have submitted their flushing sheets and residual records.
tasks.configuration: Scope: all zones of the annual flushing program, now field complete.

cards.label: Reconcile every zone sheet against the program plan and list any missed streets
Resample residuals at a selection of extremity sites in each zone
Compare post program residuals and complaint rates with the pre program baseline
Send crews back to any missed or still failing streets before the program closes
Compile the program report with water used, results achieved and problem areas
Carry the problem areas into next year program ranking with earlier dates

tasks.explanation: Close out is verification, not filing: sheets are reconciled, independent resamples test the crews results, and failures are reflushed while the program is still open. The report and the carry forward list turn one season of work into the next season plan.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for completing the annual water loss audit for the whole system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The audit follows a standard water balance method with supplied, billed and loss volumes.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one audit year using production, billing and operations records.

cards.label: Total the water supplied into the system from treatment and purchase records
Total the billed metered and billed unmetered consumption from the billing system
Estimate the unbilled authorized uses, including flushing, firefighting and municipal use
Calculate the remaining volume as water losses and split it between apparent and real losses using test data
Compare the loss percentages with previous years and with the program targets
Present the audit with the top loss reduction actions for the coming year

tasks.explanation: A water balance only works in order: supply first, then every authorized use, and losses are what remains. Splitting apparent from real losses decides whether the fix is meters or mains, and the audit ends in actions, not just percentages.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for establishing a district metered area for leakage monitoring.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The district has two feeds and several boundary valves in unknown condition.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one district of about 2,000 homes to be isolated behind a district meter.

cards.label: Define the district boundary on the map and list every feed and boundary valve
Test each boundary valve for tight closure and repair any that pass water
Install the district meter and logger on the remaining open feed
Record the district demand pattern for a baseline period with the boundary proven closed
Calculate the first minimum night flow and compare it with the expected legitimate night use
Hand the district to the leakage program with its baseline and boundary records

tasks.explanation: A district metered area is only as good as its boundary: a passing valve makes every night flow number a lie. Baseline recording follows proof of closure, and the first night flow is judged against legitimate use, not against zero.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a minimum night flow analysis in a district metered area.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The district boundary was proven closed at the start of the logging period.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one district with a full month of logged inflow data.

cards.label: Extract the lowest inflow hour for each night in the period and list the values
Estimate the legitimate night use from the customer types in the district
Subtract the legitimate use to estimate the leakage component of night flow
Convert the leakage rate into a daily loss volume for the district
Rank the district against the other districts by loss per kilometre of main
Decide whether the district goes forward to step testing or stays on monitoring

tasks.explanation: Night flow is useful because legitimate use is at its smallest and steadiest. The analysis removes that legitimate part honestly, converts what is left into a volume management can act on, and ranking spends the step testing budget where losses are worst.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for running an acoustic leak survey in a high loss district.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The district minimum night flow ranks it among the worst in the system.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one district scheduled for a full listening survey over two weeks.

cards.label: Divide the district into daily survey sections covering every valve and hydrant listening point
Listen at each fitting with the acoustic equipment and mark every suspect noise with its strength
Return to the strongest suspects in quiet hours and confirm them by listening at two points
Correlate or pinpoint the confirmed leaks and raise repair orders in priority order
Record the survey coverage and the leaks found on the district record
Re measure night flow after the repairs and report the change to the leakage program

tasks.explanation: Coverage comes before findings: a survey that skips fittings cannot claim the district is clear. Suspects are confirmed in quiet conditions before crews dig, and the post repair night flow is the only honest score for the survey.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for step testing a district to localize a leak to one section.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The test is done at night when legitimate use is lowest and steadiest.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one district losing water at night, divided into six valved sections.

cards.label: Record the district inflow with all sections open as the starting night flow
Close the first section valves and record the drop in district inflow
Close each following section in turn, recording the inflow after each closure
Reopen all sections in reverse order and confirm the inflow returns to the starting value
Rank the sections by the size of the drop each closure produced
Send the acoustic crew to the section with the largest drop first

tasks.explanation: Each closure removes one section from the total, so the size of each drop is that section loss. Reopening in reverse proves the test itself did not change the system, and the ranking sends the listening crew to the section the numbers indict.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for pinpointing a suspected leak on a trunk main using correlators.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The section has no branches and the pipe material and diameter are known.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one trunk main section between two access points where a leak noise was heard.

cards.label: Confirm the leak noise at both access points and record its strength at each
Enter the pipe material, diameter and the measured distance between the access points
Place the correlator sensors on both access points and run the correlation
Mark the indicated leak position on the surface and verify it with a ground microphone
Excavate a test hole at the marked position if the surface evidence agrees
Record the correlation result against the actual repair location to build crew confidence in the method

tasks.explanation: Correlation is arithmetic plus field craft: distance and material set the sound speed, the sensors do the timing, and a ground microphone confirms before anyone digs. Recording the result against the real location keeps the method honest over time.

tasks.prompt: Order the leadership steps when one zone demand rises sharply with no matching weather or growth explanation.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. No large new customer has connected and treatment records confirm the meter readings.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a zone using about twenty percent more water than the same period last year.

cards.label: Verify the zone meter and compare it with the storage change over the same period
Check for open interzone valves or changed boundary positions feeding water out of the zone
Review hydrant permits, flushing records and construction water use in the zone
Compare district night flows inside the zone to find where the increase concentrates
Deploy leak survey crews to the district with the largest night flow increase
Report the cause found and the volume involved to management with the recovery plan

tasks.explanation: The meter is doubted first because every later step trusts it. Boundary valves and authorized uses are checked from records before crews are deployed, night flow comparison aims the survey, and management hears the cause with a volume attached.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for running the annual large meter accuracy testing program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. Large meters drive most of the billed volume, so small errors carry large revenue effects.
tasks.configuration: Scope: the fifty largest customer meters in the system.

cards.label: Rank the large meters by consumption and time since the last accuracy test
Schedule tests with the customers to avoid their critical operating periods
Test each meter at low, medium and high flow rates and record the accuracy at each
Calculate the billing effect of each meter error from its consumption record
Repair or replace the meters whose error exceeds the program limit, starting with the largest billing effect
Adjust the program test interval based on how fast each meter type drifts

tasks.explanation: Ranking by consumption and test age spends the program where error costs most. Testing across flow rates matters because large meters fail first at low flows, and the billing calculation, not the error percentage alone, sets the repair order.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for investigating apparent losses found in the annual water audit.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. Apparent losses include meter under registration, billing errors and unauthorized use.
tasks.configuration: Scope: an audit year where apparent losses rose while real losses stayed flat.

cards.label: Compare the audit apparent loss figure with the meter testing results for the year
Audit a sample of billing accounts for missed, estimated or wrongly classified readings
Check the new meter exchange records for meters installed but not yet billing
Review unauthorized use reports, including hydrant use without permits
Correct the billing and records faults found and estimate the recovered volume
Report the findings and set the control that prevents each fault from recurring

tasks.explanation: Apparent loss is lost on paper, so the investigation works through meters, bills and records rather than pipes. Each fault found gets a volume and a control, because a one time correction without a control is next year finding repeated.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for prioritizing the leak repair backlog and reporting program results.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. Crew capacity allows only part of the backlog to be repaired each week.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a backlog of confirmed leaks of different sizes, ages and locations.

cards.label: Estimate the loss rate of each leak from the survey and correlation records
Rank the leaks by loss rate, risk to property and pavement, and safety concerns
Schedule the highest ranked leaks first and group nearby smaller leaks into the same mobilization
Track the estimated volume saved as each repair is completed
Re measure district night flows monthly to confirm the savings are real
Report the backlog, savings and remaining losses to management each quarter

tasks.explanation: The biggest and riskiest leaks go first, but nearby small leaks ride along because the crew is already there. Saved volumes are estimates until night flows confirm them, and quarterly reporting keeps the backlog visible instead of letting it age quietly.

tasks.prompt: Order the leadership steps for establishing control at a major trunk main break.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The overall responsible operator or designate acts as the incident lead.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a trunk main break flooding a major road, with a large area losing pressure.

cards.label: Confirm the break location and size from the first crew report and SCADA pressure loss
Assign the incident roles: operations lead, site crew lead and communications contact
Order the isolation plan and approve any interzone transfers needed to support the area
Notify the health unit, the municipality and affected critical customers of the outage
Set the public information line and the update interval for the duration of the event
Review progress at set intervals and approve the move from emergency response to planned repair

tasks.explanation: Command is established before tactics multiply: roles, isolation authority and notifications are set in the first decisions. Public updates run on a promised interval, and the shift from emergency to planned repair is a deliberate approval, not drift.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for isolating a trunk main break that needs valves in two zones.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. Closing the valves will drop pressure in parts of both zones.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one break on a zone boundary trunk main with no single valve pair isolating it.

cards.label: Identify every valve needed to stop flow to the break from the system map
Notify both zone crews and the control room of the isolation sequence and timing
Close the valves on the highest pressure side first, slowly, to limit surge
Close the remaining valves and confirm flow at the break has stopped or slowed to a safe level
Open a hydrant or blow off in the isolated section to drain it and prove zero energy
Tag every closed valve and log the closure order and times

tasks.explanation: A boundary break needs a sequence, not a scramble: every valve is identified before any valve moves. The high pressure side closes first and slowly, drainage proves the section is safe to work on, and tags and logs protect the crew from a well meaning reopening.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for returning a repaired trunk main to service with leadership sign off.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The repair is complete and the section has been flushed and disinfected.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one repaired trunk main section that was disinfected after the repair.

cards.label: Confirm the disinfection contact time and the flushing records for the section
Collect bacteriological samples and chlorine residuals from the repaired section
Review the sample results and approve the return only if they are satisfactory
Reopen the isolation valves slowly in the reverse order of the isolation log
Flush the downstream extremities and confirm normal residuals and pressures
Sign the return to service record and close the customer and health unit notifications

tasks.explanation: Return to service is a sign off, not a habit: disinfection and flushing records are reviewed, samples gate the decision, and valves reopen slowly in the logged reverse order. Notifications close only after normal quality is confirmed downstream.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for activating an emergency interconnection with a neighbouring municipality.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. A major break has cut the normal supply to one zone for an extended period.
tasks.configuration: Scope: an interconnection that is normally closed and covered by a mutual supply agreement.

cards.label: Confirm the size and expected duration of the supply shortfall in the affected zone
Contact the neighbouring municipality duty officer and request activation under the agreement
Agree the flow rate, the duration and the metering and water quality checks to be used
Open the interconnection slowly and confirm flow direction and pressures on both sides
Sample chlorine residuals on both sides of the interconnection during the supply period
Close the interconnection when normal supply returns and reconcile the volume supplied for the agreement record

tasks.explanation: The agreement governs the emergency: the request, rates and quality checks are agreed before valves move, because two systems are affected by every decision. Slow opening protects both systems, and volume reconciliation closes the agreement properly.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for coordinating a boil water advisory after a major depressurization event.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The medical officer of health directs whether an advisory is issued.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one neighbourhood that lost pressure completely during a trunk main break.

cards.label: Provide the health unit with the affected area map, the cause and the expected duration
Issue the advisory through the municipal channels exactly as directed by the health unit
Restore pressure, then flush and disinfect the affected mains as directed
Collect the required bacteriological samples from the affected area on the required schedule
Provide the results to the health unit and lift the advisory only on their direction
File the complete advisory record with the incident report and the sampling results

tasks.explanation: The health unit owns the advisory decision, so the operator first job is accurate information: area, cause and duration. Restoration and sampling follow their direction, the advisory lifts only on their word, and the full record files together so the event can be audited as one story.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for notifying critical customers during a major unplanned outage.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The critical customer contact list is maintained by customer service and verified each year.
tasks.configuration: Scope: an outage affecting a hospital, two nursing homes and a food plant in one zone.

cards.label: Confirm the outage area and the expected duration from the incident lead
Pull the critical customer list for the affected area and assign a caller to each facility
Call each facility with the cause, the expected duration and the conservation steps requested
Record the name of the person reached at each facility and any special needs they report
Update each facility at the promised intervals and immediately if the duration changes
Call each facility when supply is restored and record the close out in the incident log

tasks.explanation: Critical customers are called by a person, not reached by a broadcast: each facility gets a named caller, a cause and a duration. Special needs flow back to the incident lead, updates keep the promise made in the first call, and restoration is confirmed facility by facility.

tasks.prompt: Order the leadership steps for managing flooding and property damage at a major break site.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. Municipal risk and insurance staff handle claims after the event.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a break that has flooded a road, undermined pavement and entered two basements.

cards.label: Make the site safe with road closure, traffic control and utility checks before repair work expands
Stop the water by completing the isolation, then start dewatering of flooded areas
Photograph and record the damage and the water levels before cleanup alters the scene
Provide the affected property owners with the municipal claims contact information
Check the undermined pavement and excavate only after it is confirmed stable
File the site record, photographs and owner contacts with the incident report

tasks.explanation: Safety and water control come first, but the damage record is made before cleanup erases it, because owners and insurers will ask questions the crew memory cannot answer later. Owners receive the claims route directly, and pavement stability gates the excavation.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for triaging repair resources when three breaks occur during one storm event.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The overall responsible operator directs the triage decisions.
tasks.configuration: Scope: three breaks of different sizes across two zones, with two repair crews available.

cards.label: Collect the size, location, customers affected and safety risk for each break
Rank the breaks by safety risk first, then by customers out and loss rate
Assign the first crew to the highest ranked break and the second crew to the next
Isolate the third break to stop its loss and schedule it with a clear public message about timing
Borrow or contract additional crew capacity if the third break risk grows
Review the ranking whenever a repair finishes or conditions change and reassign crews as needed

tasks.explanation: Triage ranks by safety before convenience, and the break that waits is still isolated and honestly messaged rather than left running and unmentioned. The ranking is a living decision that changes as crews free up, not a verdict made once in the office.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for the post incident debrief after a major main break event.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. Crews, control room staff and customer service all took part in the response.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a debrief held within one week of a trunk main break that caused a large outage.

cards.label: Reconstruct the event timeline from SCADA records, logs and call records
Identify what worked, including decisions and equipment that performed well
Identify the failures and delays, including valve problems, information gaps and resource limits
Agree a corrective action for each failure with an owner and a due date
Enter the actions into the tracking system and brief management on the list
Verify completion of the actions at the following monthly operations review

tasks.explanation: A debrief built on records rather than recollection finds the real delays. Successes are recorded so they are repeated, failures become owned and dated actions rather than complaints, and verification at the monthly review is what separates a debrief from a discussion.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for deploying a portable generator to a booster station during a power outage.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The outage duration is unknown and the portable generator is stored at the works yard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one booster station without power, serving a zone with about six hours of storage.

cards.label: Confirm the outage scope with the utility and estimate the zone storage time remaining
Dispatch the generator and a qualified operator to the station before storage reaches its critical level
Connect the generator using the station transfer switch and confirm correct rotation and voltage
Start the duty pump on generator power and confirm discharge pressure and flow
Set a refuelling schedule and a staffing watch for as long as the generator runs
Return the station to utility power when it is stable and record the run hours and fuel used

tasks.explanation: Storage time is the clock: the generator moves while there is still margin, not when the tanks are empty. Connection checks protect the pump motor, refuelling and staffing are planned for an outage of unknown length, and the return to utility power is recorded like any other operation.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for running the annual cross connection survey cycle for commercial and industrial properties.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The program operates under the municipal cross connection control bylaw.
tasks.configuration: Scope: the program year survey list drawn from the property and business licence records.

cards.label: Build the survey list from new businesses, changed uses and properties due for resurvey
Assign surveys by hazard level, with the highest hazard properties scheduled first
Complete the surveys and record every cross connection found and its hazard rating
Issue each property its required protection, ranging from a device to premises isolation
Set the device installation and first test deadlines in the compliance letters
Enter every result into the program database and report cycle completion to management

tasks.explanation: The list is built from change, because new and changed uses create new hazards. Hazard order sets the schedule, surveys produce requirements rather than advice, and deadlines plus database entry turn field work into an enforceable program.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for scheduling annual backflow tests for high hazard premises.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. Only certified testers with calibrated test kits may perform program tests.
tasks.configuration: Scope: high hazard properties whose devices are due for annual testing this quarter.

cards.label: Pull the list of high hazard devices coming due in the quarter from the database
Send test due notices to the property owners with the tester requirements stated
Confirm each tester certification and test kit calibration record as reports arrive
Receive and review the test reports for completeness and correct device information
Follow up any property whose report has not arrived ten days before its deadline
Record the passed tests and carry any failures into the failure response process

tasks.explanation: Notices go out early enough for owners to hire a tester, and tester credentials are verified as reports arrive rather than assumed. The follow up before the deadline, not after it, is what keeps high hazard compliance near complete.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps after a backflow preventer fails its annual test at a high hazard property.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The device protects against a high hazard and the bylaw sets repair timelines.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one failed test on a reduced pressure device protecting a chemical using facility.

cards.label: Confirm the failure details with the tester, including which check valve or relief valve failed
Issue the repair notice with the bylaw deadline for a high hazard failure
Require the property to control the hazard in the interim, such as by disconnecting the risk use if directed
Verify the repair or replacement is completed by a certified tester retest
Receive and file the passing retest report and update the device record
Escalate to enforcement if the deadline passes without a passing retest

tasks.explanation: A failed device at a high hazard site is an open door to the distribution system, so the response runs on the bylaw clock. Interim hazard control protects the system while repair proceeds, the retest proves the fix, and enforcement is the stated consequence, not a surprise.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for assessing backflow protection for a new industrial water connection.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The assessment happens before the service is connected.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a new food processing plant applying for a large water service.

cards.label: Obtain the plant water use description, including chemicals, boilers and process connections
Assign the hazard rating for the facility using the program hazard table
Decide whether device protection at the process or premises isolation at the property line is required
Specify the device type, size and installation standard in the connection approval
Inspect the installation and witness the first test before the service is put into use
Enter the device into the testing database with its first annual test date

tasks.explanation: Protection is decided from what the plant actually does with water, before the service exists to argue about. Premises isolation is chosen when internal protection cannot be trusted to cover every use, and the device enters the testing program from its first day, not from its first failure.

tasks.prompt: Order the leadership steps after a suspected backflow incident affects water quality near an industrial property.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The cause is not yet confirmed and the industrial property has a history of overdue tests.
tasks.configuration: Scope: discoloured and chemical tasting water reported by neighbours of one industrial site.

cards.label: Isolate the suspect property service if the risk justifies it and notify the property operator
Sample the mains around the property for residuals and the suspected contaminant indicators
Check the property backflow records and inspect its protection devices with the owner
Flush the affected mains and resample until results confirm normal quality
Notify the health unit if there is any indication drinking water was contaminated
Require the corrective protection work and file the incident with the program enforcement record

tasks.explanation: Isolation and sampling protect the public while the cause is still a suspicion. Records and inspection test that suspicion against the property actual protection, the health unit is engaged on indication rather than proof, and corrective work plus the enforcement record close the loop.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for the annual verification of backflow tester certifications and test kit calibrations.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The program accepts reports only from testers meeting the bylaw requirements.
tasks.configuration: Scope: every tester who submitted program test reports in the past year.

cards.label: List every tester who submitted reports during the year from the program database
Request current certification copies and test kit calibration certificates from each tester
Compare the documents received against the reports each tester submitted
Suspend acceptance of reports from any tester whose documents are missing or expired
Notify the suspended testers and the affected property owners of the change
File the verified tester list and publish it for property owners to use

tasks.explanation: Reports are only as good as the tester and the kit behind them, so verification works from the reports actually submitted. Suspension protects owners from paying for reports the program cannot accept, and owners are told directly so they can hire a listed tester in time.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for surveying municipal facilities under the cross connection program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. Municipal facilities are surveyed to the same standard as private properties.
tasks.configuration: Scope: arenas, pools, works yards and community centres owned by the municipality.

cards.label: Inventory every municipal facility water use, including pools, boilers, irrigation and vehicle washing
Survey each facility and rate the hazard of every cross connection found
Install or upgrade the required devices using the capital or maintenance budget line assigned
Test every new and existing device and enter the results in the program database
Set the resurvey and test dates so the facilities stay in the normal program cycle
Report the municipal compliance status alongside the private property results

tasks.explanation: The program credibility depends on the municipality meeting its own bylaw, so its facilities are inventoried and surveyed like any other property. Devices enter the same database and cycle, and municipal results are reported in the open, beside the private results.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for auditing temporary water connections, including hydrant permits and construction filling points.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. Temporary connections require a meter and backflow protection under the permit conditions.
tasks.configuration: Scope: all active temporary connections issued in the current construction season.

cards.label: List every active hydrant permit and construction filling point from the permit records
Visit each site and confirm the meter and backflow preventer are installed as permitted
Check for unpermitted connections found during the site visits
Bill or correct the meter readings for the connections inspected
Issue warnings or penalties for connections missing the required protection
Close or renew each permit at season end and file the audit results

tasks.explanation: Temporary connections are real connections: the audit starts from the permit list but looks for the unpermitted ones too. Protection is verified in the field rather than on the application form, and season end closure prevents forgotten connections from becoming permanent risks.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for clearing a backlog of overdue backflow tests found in a database audit.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The backlog built up over two years of staff turnover in the program office.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a backlog of overdue devices across all hazard levels.

cards.label: Sort the overdue devices by hazard level and by how long each test is overdue
Send compliance notices to the highest hazard and longest overdue properties first
Offer a short catch up window with clear deadlines before enforcement begins
Process the returning test reports daily and update the compliance status as they arrive
Escalate the remaining non responders through the bylaw enforcement steps in order
Report the cleared and remaining counts to management monthly until the backlog is gone

tasks.explanation: Hazard and age set the order, because the oldest high hazard gap is the largest risk. A defined catch up window is fair and produces most of the reports, enforcement handles the rest in bylaw order, and monthly reporting keeps the backlog from going quiet again.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for moving a non compliant high hazard property to premises isolation.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The bylaw allows the municipality to require premises isolation and to restrict service for continued non compliance.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one high hazard property that has ignored repeated device repair and test notices.

cards.label: Confirm the full notice and enforcement history for the property from the program file
Issue the final notice requiring premises isolation by a set date, with the bylaw basis stated
Meet the property owner to explain the device required and the consequences of the deadline passing
Inspect the isolation device installation and witness its first test when it is installed
If the deadline passes without compliance, apply the service restriction steps in the bylaw in order
Record the outcome in the enforcement file and set the annual test cycle for the new device

tasks.explanation: Isolation is the end of a documented road, not a first reaction: the file must show every notice given. The owner hears the requirement and the consequence in person, the installed device is witnessed like any other, and the bylaw steps are followed in order so the action stands up.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for using main break records to prioritize the watermain renewal capital list.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. Break records include location, main material, age, diameter and repair cost.
tasks.configuration: Scope: five years of break records for the whole distribution system.

cards.label: Clean the break records and confirm every break is tied to the correct main asset
Calculate the break rate for each main segment over the five year period
Combine the break rate with the age, material and consequence of failure for each segment
Rank the segments and field verify the condition of the highest ranked candidates
Build the renewal list in ranked order with the estimated cost of each project
Present the list with the break evidence for each project to the capital review

tasks.explanation: Capital money follows evidence: records are cleaned before rates are calculated, break history is combined with consequence because a quiet trunk main can matter more than a noisy small main, and every project on the list carries the evidence that put it there.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for assessing valve criticality across the distribution system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. A critical valve is one whose failure to operate would greatly extend an outage.
tasks.configuration: Scope: all transmission and distribution valves, ranked for the exercising and replacement programs.

cards.label: Identify the valves that isolate trunk mains, storage facilities and critical customers
For each valve, determine the area and customer count that an extended outage would affect
Combine that consequence with the valve operating history and condition records
Rank the valves and set a shorter exercising interval for the most critical ones
Schedule replacement or repair for critical valves with poor operating records
Load the criticality ranking into the asset system so isolation planning uses it

tasks.explanation: Criticality is consequence meeting condition: a valve matters because of what its failure would strand. The ranking changes real behaviour, through shorter exercising intervals, earlier replacement and isolation plans that check critical valves first.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for integrating hydrant inspection results into the asset management program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. Hydrants are inspected annually and flow tested on a rotating cycle.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one year of hydrant inspection and flow test results for the whole system.

cards.label: Compile the inspection deficiencies by type, including drainage, operation, caps and coating
Separate the deficiencies into safety and fire protection items and cosmetic items
Raise repair work orders for the fire protection items in priority order by area risk
Calculate the replacement candidates from age, condition and parts availability
Feed the replacement list and the repair costs into the asset plan for the next budget
Report the percentage of hydrants fully available for fire protection to management

tasks.explanation: Inspection data only matters when it becomes work and money decisions. Fire protection deficiencies outrank cosmetics, replacement is argued from age and parts as well as condition, and the availability percentage is the number management and the fire department actually need.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for the annual watermain renewal planning workshop.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. Each group brings its own data set to the workshop.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one workshop with operations, engineering and finance staff setting the five year renewal program.

cards.label: Circulate the break analysis, condition results and growth forecasts before the workshop
Agree the ranking criteria and their weights at the start of the session
Score the candidate projects against the agreed criteria as a group
Fit the scored projects into the five year funding envelope year by year
Record the projects deferred and the risk accepted by deferring each one
Issue the agreed program and the deferred list to all participants after the workshop

tasks.explanation: Criteria are agreed before projects are scored, so the argument is about weights rather than favourites. Deferred projects are recorded with their risk, because a deferral is a decision someone owns, and the issued program is the single version everyone works from.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for accepting new subdivision water assets into municipal ownership.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. Assumption follows the municipal subdivision agreement and standards.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one completed subdivision with mains, valves, hydrants and services built by a developer.

cards.label: Receive and review the record drawings and the valve and hydrant data sheets
Inspect the assets in the field against the drawings, operating every valve and hydrant
Confirm pressure test, disinfection and sampling records are complete and satisfactory
List every deficiency and hold the security until the developer corrects them
Enter the accepted assets into the asset registry, maps and maintenance programs
Set the warranty inspection date and notify operations that the assets are now municipal

tasks.explanation: Paper and field must agree before the municipality owns the problem: drawings are checked by operating the actual valves and hydrants. Deficiencies are held against security while leverage exists, and registry entry plus program enrolment make the assets maintained rather than merely owned.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for building the lead service line inventory for the older parts of the system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The inventory supports the lead sampling program and the replacement plan.
tasks.configuration: Scope: an inventory covering homes built before the era when lead services were discontinued locally.

cards.label: Identify the age bands and neighbourhoods where lead services are likely from building records
Check the municipal service records and past repair notes for material information
Inspect the service material at the curb stop or meter during other planned work in the area
Send owners in the target area a short survey and scratch test instructions for their service pipe
Combine all sources into the inventory with a confidence level for each record
Use the inventory to target sampling sites and to build the replacement priority list

tasks.explanation: No single source knows the inventory, so records, field checks and owners each contribute, and confidence levels keep a guess from being treated as a fact. The inventory earns its keep by aiming sampling and replacement money at the homes most likely to have lead.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for planning an inspection of a trunk main river crossing.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The crossing is a single feed to the zone beyond the river.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one river crossing main that has never been internally inspected.

cards.label: Review the crossing drawings, age, material and any past leak or movement records
Assess the consequence of failure and the repair access limits at the crossing
Select the inspection method that suits the pipe and the access points available
Plan the zone supply support needed while the crossing is out of service for inspection
Schedule the work for the low flow season and obtain the environmental and access permissions
Issue the inspection plan with the contingency for an emergency repair if a defect is found

tasks.explanation: A single feed crossing is inspected as a risk project, not a routine job: consequence and access shape the method, the zone beyond the river needs a supply plan, and the contingency for finding a serious defect is written before the pipe is opened.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for procuring a structural condition assessment of an aging reservoir.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The assessment will inform a rehabilitation or replacement decision in the capital plan.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one ground reservoir showing coating failure and concrete cracking.

cards.label: Write the scope covering structure, coating, roof, fittings and remaining service life
Invite proposals from qualified inspection firms with potable water reservoir experience
Evaluate the proposals on method, experience and price using the municipal scoring sheet
Award the work and hold the pre work meeting on outage, entry and disinfection requirements
Receive the draft report and review the findings and recommendations with the firm
Enter the condition rating and the recommended work into the asset plan with cost estimates

tasks.explanation: The scope decides what the report can conclude, so remaining life and every major element are named in it. Evaluation is scored rather than improvised, the outage and water quality rules are settled before entry, and the rating lands in the asset plan where it can compete for funding.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for auditing asset registry data quality before the capital forecast is updated.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The forecast uses age, material and condition fields from the registry.
tasks.configuration: Scope: the registry records for mains, valves, hydrants and storage facilities.

cards.label: Extract the registry fields the forecast depends on and count the missing or default values
Sample records from each asset type and verify them against maps and field checks
Correct the systematic errors found, such as wrong install decades or materials
Flag the records that cannot be verified and exclude them from the forecast averages
Re run the forecast inputs and compare the change with the previous forecast
Report the data quality limits alongside the forecast so decisions carry the right confidence

tasks.explanation: A forecast built on default ages and guessed materials looks precise and is not. Sampling and field verification measure the error, systematic faults are fixed at the source, and the quality limits travel with the forecast so confidence is honest.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for safely decommissioning an abandoned section of watermain.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The new main is in service and all customers have been transferred to it.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one replaced main section that is to be abandoned in place.

cards.label: Confirm every service and connection has been transferred off the old main
Close and tag the valves connecting the old main to the live system
Drain the old main and cut and cap its ends at the connection points
Remove or fill the valve boxes and hydrant leads so no live connection remains hidden
Update the maps and asset registry to show the main as abandoned with the date
Record the abandonment details so future excavators can identify the pipe they find

tasks.explanation: Abandonment fails when a hidden live connection survives, so transfer is confirmed service by service before cutting begins. Physical separation at every connection, surface cleanup and honest mapping protect both the live system and the next crew that digs there.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for an energy audit of the distribution pumping stations.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. Energy records are available from utility bills and station run hour logs.
tasks.configuration: Scope: all booster and transfer pumping stations for one audit year.

cards.label: Total the energy used and its cost for each station from the utility records
Total the volume pumped by each station from the flow and run hour records
Calculate the energy used per unit volume for each station
Rank the stations and compare the worst performers with their pump test results
Investigate the worst station for worn pumps, throttled valves or poor scheduling
Present the audit with the savings actions ranked by payback

tasks.explanation: Energy per unit volume is the comparison that matters, because raw bills only show which station is biggest. The worst ratio leads to a physical investigation rather than a scolding, and actions are ranked by payback so the audit becomes a work list.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for moving pumping to off peak electricity hours without risking storage or pressure.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The electricity rate has time of use pricing with a large off peak discount.
tasks.configuration: Scope: the filling schedules for the main storage facilities.

cards.label: Analyse the current filling times against the rate periods and the demand pattern
Set target morning storage levels that let the tanks coast through the peak rate hours
Reschedule filling into the off peak window in stages, one facility at a time
Confirm zone pressures and fire storage stay inside limits at the new schedule
Compare the first month energy cost with the same month pattern before the change
Lock the proven schedule into the control system and record the savings in the energy file

tasks.explanation: The tanks are the battery: morning levels are set so storage, not peak power, carries the expensive hours. Staged changes keep one facility mistake from becoming a system problem, and the cost comparison proves the schedule change rather than assuming it.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for deciding whether to overhaul a booster pump with declining efficiency.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The pump is one of three at its station, so it can be taken out of service.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one large booster pump whose energy per unit volume has risen over two years.

cards.label: Confirm the decline from the station energy and flow records over the two years
Run a pump test measuring flow, head and power against the original duty point
Inspect the wear points the test implicates, such as wear rings and impeller condition
Price the overhaul and estimate the energy savings from the restored efficiency
Compare the overhaul cost and savings with the replacement cost and savings
Make and record the decision and schedule the work in the low demand season

tasks.explanation: Records raise the question and a pump test answers it, because energy drift can also come from changed duty. The overhaul case is made on measured savings against both doing nothing and replacing, and the work is timed to the season when the station can spare the pump.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for the overall responsible operator daily review of the distribution system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The review is a duty of the overall responsible operator under Ontario Regulation 170/03.
tasks.configuration: Scope: the daily review covering all zones, storage, water quality and staffing.

cards.label: Review the overnight SCADA alarms, storage levels and zone pressures
Review the latest chlorine residuals and any adverse or pending sample results
Check the day planned work, isolations and customer notifications in progress
Confirm certified operator coverage for every shift and facility for the next 24 hours
Direct any corrective actions and assign them to named operators with times
Sign the daily review entry in the operating log

tasks.explanation: The daily review connects the whole system in one pass: plant state, water quality, planned work and people. Coverage is checked before it becomes a gap, actions are assigned to names with times, and the signed entry is the record that the duty was actually performed.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for verifying certified operator coverage for a holiday period.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. Ontario Regulation 170/03 requires certified operators and an overall responsible operator at all times.
tasks.configuration: Scope: two weeks of holiday schedules across all distribution shifts and facilities.

cards.label: List every shift and facility needing coverage in the holiday period, including on call duties
Match the scheduled operators against their certification level and expiry dates
Identify the gaps and shifts covered by an operator whose certificate expires inside the period
Fill the gaps by approved swaps or overtime and name the backup overall responsible operator
Post the confirmed schedule and notify every affected operator personally
File the coverage record with the certification copies for the period

tasks.explanation: Coverage is verified against certificates, not names on a roster: an expired certificate is a gap even when a person is present. The backup overall responsible operator is named before the holiday, and personal notification prevents the schedule from being a surprise.

tasks.prompt: Order the leadership steps when a SCADA communication failure blinds the control room to several facilities.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. Field staff can operate every affected facility manually.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a communication outage affecting two reservoirs and one booster station for an unknown duration.

cards.label: Confirm which facilities and data points are lost and that the failure is communications, not process
Dispatch operators to the affected facilities to read levels and pressures in person
Place filling and pumping on manual control using the posted facility instructions
Set a reporting interval for field readings to the control room by phone or radio
Log all manual operations and readings as the official record for the outage period
Return to automatic control facility by facility as communications are restored and reconcile the records

tasks.explanation: The first distinction is between losing sight of the system and losing the system itself. Manual control with written instructions and a set reporting rhythm replaces the screen, the log becomes the official record, and restoration is staged so each facility is proven before it is trusted.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for preparing and running the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard management review for distribution.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. Top management attends and the review outputs become tracked commitments.
tasks.configuration: Scope: the annual review covering incidents, audits, maintenance and improvement actions.

cards.label: Collect the review inputs: incident summaries, audit findings, sampling results and maintenance completion
Summarize the status of the improvement actions from the previous review
Present the inputs and the trends to management in the review meeting
Agree the new improvement actions, owners, resources and due dates in the meeting
Record the review minutes and enter the actions into the tracking system
Report progress on the actions at the monthly operations meetings until they close

tasks.explanation: A management review runs on prepared inputs, not impressions: incidents, audits and last year promises are assembled first. Actions agreed without owners and resources are wishes, so the meeting fixes all three, and monthly reporting keeps the commitments alive between reviews.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for responding to findings in a Ministry inspection report for the distribution system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. Each finding carries a response expectation and some carry required actions with dates.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one inspection report containing several findings and recommended actions.

cards.label: Read the report in full and list every finding and required action with its date
Assign an owner and a corrective action plan for each finding
Complete the required actions by their dates and keep the evidence for each one
Reply to the Ministry in writing describing the action taken for every finding
Enter the findings into the corrective action tracking system
Review the same areas in the next internal audit to confirm the fixes held

tasks.explanation: The report is answered finding by finding, with dates driving the order of work. Evidence is kept as each action completes because memory is not proof, the written reply closes the Ministry loop, and the next internal audit checks the fix rather than the promise.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for signing off a newly promoted operator on independent zone operations.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03. The operator holds the required certificate and has completed supervised shifts.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one operator moving to independent shift duties covering zones and storage.

cards.label: Review the training record and list the tasks the operator must demonstrate
Have the operator run a full zone round, including storage checks and a valve operation, under observation
Have the operator handle a simulated low pressure event and an adverse result notification drill
Correct any gaps found with further supervised practice on those tasks only
Sign the competency record and set the date from which independent duties begin
Schedule the first month of independent shifts with an experienced operator on call as backup

tasks.explanation: Sign off is by demonstration, not by time served: the operator runs the real round and the drills that carry the real risk. Gaps are retrained specifically rather than generally, and early independent shifts carry a named backup while confidence becomes experience.

tasks.prompt: A chloraminated Ontario system sees free ammonia rising and nitrite appearing in one elevated tank while all other tanks stay clean.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional multi tank chloraminated system. Tank sampling at inlet, outlet and depth points is available, with paired zones for comparison.

evidence.label: Tank C outlet nitrite reads 0.18 mg/L as N while its inlet reads 0.01 mg/L on the same day.
Free ammonia in Tank C has fallen from 0.45 to 0.12 mg/L over three weeks while total chlorine fell from 1.8 to 0.7 mg/L.
Tank C level cycles only between 82 and 94 percent, giving an estimated water age over 9 days, while Tank B cycles deeply and keeps age under 3 days.
Tank B, fed the same water, shows nitrite below detection and stable residuals.
A trial deep cycling and drawdown of Tank C drops nitrite to 0.03 mg/L and restores total chlorine to 1.4 mg/L within a week.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Nitrification is active inside Tank C, driven by long water age from shallow cycling, consuming chloramine and producing nitrite
The treatment plant has started overdosing ammonia for the whole system
A laboratory error is producing false nitrite results for Tank C only
A cross connection is feeding untreated water into Tank C

inference.explanation: Only in tank nitrification fits nitrite forming across the tank itself, falling free ammonia and total chlorine, long age from shallow cycling, a clean paired tank on the same water, and recovery after deep cycling. A plant dosing change or lab error would affect Tank B too, and untreated inflow would dilute rather than create this pattern.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Trend Tank C nitrite, free ammonia and total chlorine daily during a set deep cycling program and log water age
Raise the plant chloramine dose for the entire system and wait a month
Take Tank C out of service permanently without further sampling

nextClue.explanation: Daily trending during deep cycling directly tests whether reducing water age reverses nitrification, which is the control the evidence points to.

clueText.nc-a: Nitrite falls steadily as cycling deepens and age drops below 4 days, confirming age driven nitrification and the fix.
clueText.nc-b: Tank B stays clean on the same plant dose, so a system wide dose increase is not supported.
clueText.nc-c: The tank recovered under cycling in the trial, so permanent removal is not justified before the cycling program is verified.

tasks.prompt: Two ground reservoirs in one Ontario zone age water very differently, and only the older water reservoir keeps failing residual targets at its outlet.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional paired reservoirs on the same feed. Inlet and outlet residual sampling and level records are available.

evidence.label: Reservoir 1 inlet and outlet free chlorine both read near 0.80 mg/L on paired sampling days.
Reservoir 2 inlet reads 0.82 mg/L but its outlet reads 0.22 mg/L on the same days.
Reservoir 2 operates between 88 and 97 percent full with one small daily draw, while Reservoir 1 turns over about 40 percent of its volume daily.
Water temperature in Reservoir 2 is 23 C and its calculated age exceeds 8 days.
When Reservoir 2 is drawn down to 45 percent and refilled over two days in a trial, outlet residual rises to 0.61 mg/L.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The plant is underdosing chlorine for the whole zone
Reservoir 2 loses residual because its water is stored too long with almost no turnover, not because of the incoming water
Reservoir 2 has a leaking outlet valve diluting its contents
The Reservoir 2 outlet sample tap is faulty and reads low

inference.explanation: Incoming water is identical and Reservoir 1 holds residual, so plant dosing is not the cause. Residual falls across Reservoir 2 only, its age exceeds 8 days with minimal turnover, and a drawdown trial restores outlet residual. A faulty tap cannot explain the trial recovery.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Increase the plant chlorine dose until Reservoir 2 outlet complies
Set a wider operating level band for Reservoir 2 and trend paired inlet and outlet residuals for two weeks
Replace the Reservoir 2 outlet sample tap and close the case

nextClue.explanation: A wider level band attacks the proven cause, long storage, and paired trending verifies the outlet holds residual under normal operation.

clueText.nc-a: Reservoir 1 already holds 0.80 mg/L on the current dose, so raising the dose would overfeed the rest of the zone.
clueText.nc-b: Outlet residual holds above 0.55 mg/L for two weeks under the wider band, confirming turnover was the controlling factor.
clueText.nc-c: A second flushed sample agreed with the tap reading, so the tap is not the explanation.

tasks.prompt: An Ontario standpipe shows a warm, low residual layer at its base in late summer while samples from its upper sampling port look normal.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional standpipe with sampling ports at three heights and a single common inlet and outlet pipe at the base.

evidence.label: Upper port free chlorine reads 0.70 mg/L while the base port reads 0.15 mg/L on the same morning.
Base water temperature reads 24 C while upper water reads 19 C.
The standpipe fills and draws through the same base pipe and has no internal mixer or separate inlet.
Level records show only the top 15 percent of volume exchanging daily for the past month.
A trial using a temporary portable mixer raises base residual to 0.55 mg/L and evens temperatures within days.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The base sampling port is plugged with rust and gives stale samples
Groundwater is leaking into the base of the standpipe
The standpipe is thermally stratified with a stagnant warm bottom layer, because only the top volume exchanges and there is no mixing
The plant chlorine dose drops every night

inference.explanation: A plugged port would not explain the 5 degree temperature difference or the response to mixing. Groundwater inflow would show in level and volume balance, and a nightly plant dose drop would affect the upper port too. Stratification with a stagnant base fits every observation including the mixer trial.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Replace the base sampling port and stop investigating
Lower the whole system chlorine target because the upper port is normal
Install permanent mixing or a separate inlet arrangement and profile temperature and residual by depth monthly

nextClue.explanation: Depth profiling after a mixing fix verifies the whole volume, not just the top, now exchanges and holds residual.

clueText.nc-a: The port produced free flowing fresh samples and agreed with a drained sample, so it was not plugged.
clueText.nc-b: The base layer fails residual targets, so the normal upper reading cannot set the system target.
clueText.nc-c: After mixing is installed, base and upper residuals agree within 0.08 mg/L and temperatures even out, confirming stratification is corrected.

tasks.prompt: Nitrite appears each August in one Ontario pressure zone only, always in the streets farthest from the booster chloramination station.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional chloraminated zone with a booster station at its entry. Distances, ages and seasonal sampling records are available.

evidence.label: Zone entry nitrite is below detection in all months, including August.
Far end nitrite reaches 0.22 mg/L as N in August but stays below 0.02 mg/L from November to May.

Keep the light cover reservoir empty each spring

tasks.prompt: Disinfection byproduct results climb in one Ontario zone each summer while the plant treated water results stay flat and compliant.

Move the zone sampling point next to the plant

tasks.prompt: Acoustic surveys keep flagging leak noise at the same Ontario intersection, yet two excavations there found dry soil and sound pipe.

tasks.prompt: A rural Ontario concession road shows a wet ditch all summer in a drought, with no surface break visible and homes reporting normal pressure.

Deepen the ditch so the water drains away faster

tasks.prompt: Unaccounted water spikes every December in an Ontario town, then returns to normal each January, for three years running.

tasks.prompt: A pressure zone in Ontario loses water at night, but its district meter is on a feed shared with a neighbouring zone, so night flow alone cannot prove which zone leaks.

tasks.prompt: Hydrant flow for fire protection in one Ontario neighbourhood tests well, but the water loss team insists a large leak must exist because the neighbourhood uses far more water per home than the town average.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional neighbourhood billing analysis with per connection use, meter ages and a large metered school and arena inside the boundary.

evidence.label: Average use per connection in the neighbourhood is 60 percent above the town average.
The neighbourhood boundary drawn for the analysis includes a school and an arena, both large metered users.
Residential only use, once the school and arena are removed, matches the town average closely.
Minimum night flow in the neighbourhood is normal for its size, at 2.1 L/s.
Residential meter accuracy spot tests pass within limits.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: A trunk leak is hiding because hydrant tests only run briefly
Residential meters in the neighbourhood underregister heavily
There is no large leak; the high per home figure is an artefact of dividing total use, including two large users, by home count
Homes in the neighbourhood all have leaking toilets

inference.explanation: Normal night flow rules out a large continuous leak, and residential meters pass accuracy tests. Removing the two large users brings residential use to the town average, which fully explains the figure without any leak.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Correct the analysis method to separate large users before computing per home use, and record the correction
Excavate the neighbourhood trunk main to find the hidden leak
Replace all residential meters in the neighbourhood

nextClue.explanation: A corrected method prevents the same false alarm in every district with a large user inside its boundary.

clueText.nc-a: The corrected method is applied town wide and no other district shows a false per home spike.
